title: Design a News Feed
subtitle: Watch one post reach a million timelines, and see why celebrities force a hybrid of push and pull.
learn: Fan-out on write (push) versus fan-out on read (pull), and what each costs
Why a feed is stored as a per-user list of post IDs in a cache
The celebrity problem and the hybrid that fixes it
Where the ranking stage sits and why it only scores a few hundred candidates
How to size writes per second and cache memory from a few assumptions

steps.title: What does opening the app need?
steps.body: You open the app and expect recent posts from the people you follow, newest and most relevant first, in under half a second. Assume 100 million daily users, about 200 followers each, and one post per user per day. That is roughly 100 million posts and 1 billion feed loads a day, so reads outnumber writes about 10 to 1. The design question is when to do the work of building each person's feed: when someone posts, or when someone opens the app?
steps.idea: A feed is a read-heavy join between who you follow and what they posted; the design question is when to compute it.
steps.caption: Many authors, many readers, and one costly job: joining them.

steps.title: Fan-out on read (pull)
steps.body: The simplest design builds your feed when you open the app, called fan-out on read or "pull". The feed service gets your list of followed accounts, asks the post store for each one's recent posts, merges them, and returns the top page. Writing is trivial: one row per post. But each feed load becomes hundreds of lookups. At about 11,000 feed loads per second, the post store gets crushed and each load is slow.
steps.idea: Pull makes writes cheap and reads expensive, which is backwards when reads dominate.
steps.caption: Every feed load queries the post store once per followed account.

steps.title: Fan-out on write (push)
steps.body: Flip it: do the work when a post is created. This is fan-out on write, or "push". The author saves a post, and a background job later copies the new post's ID into every follower's ready-made feed list. A queue (a waiting line for jobs) holds that job, so the post service answers "201 Created" right away and the author never waits. A 200-follower author costs 200 small writes, and none of them slow down any reader.
steps.idea: Push moves the cost from the many reads to the fewer writes, and does it in the background.
steps.caption: A new post is saved and a fan-out job is queued; the author gets 201 Created.

steps.title: Workers fill the feed cache
steps.body: Workers take the job off the queue, look up the author's followers, and add the post ID to each follower's list in the feed cache (fast in-memory storage). Each list keeps only the latest 500 IDs. We store IDs, not whole posts: 500 IDs of 8 bytes is about 4 KB per user, so 100 million users need roughly 400 GB, which fits on a modest cache cluster. At 100 million posts a day and 200 followers each, that is about 230,000 cache writes per second on average.
steps.idea: Feeds are lists of post IDs in memory; the cap keeps memory bounded and the writes cheap.
steps.caption: Workers write the new post's ID into each follower's list.

steps.title: Reading becomes a lookup
steps.body: Now opening the app is cheap. The feed service reads your ID list from the cache in a millisecond or two, then fetches the post contents for the top IDs in one batched request to the post store, and returns them. The list was built ahead of time, so the cost no longer depends on how many people you follow. Posts from deleted or blocked accounts are filtered out when you read, so a delete does not require rewriting every list.
steps.idea: Push turns a feed load into a cache read plus a batched fetch of post bodies.
steps.caption: The feed service reads a ready-made ID list, then fetches the post bodies.

steps.title: The celebrity problem
steps.body: Push breaks for accounts with huge audiences. One post from a user with 50 million followers means 50 million cache writes. At a few hundred thousand writes per second, that is minutes of backlog, which delays everyone else's posts. Most of those writes are wasted on followers who will not open the app soon. One account can create a write spike bigger than the whole system's normal load.
steps.idea: Push cost scales with follower count, so a few huge accounts can dominate total write load.
steps.caption: One celebrity post triggers tens of millions of writes, and the queue backs up.

steps.title: The hybrid
steps.body: Real systems mix both. Normal accounts use push. Accounts above a follower threshold, say 100,000 (a tunable rule of thumb), skip fan-out and are only saved. When you open the app, the feed service takes your pre-built list from the cache, pulls recent posts from the few celebrities you follow directly from the post store, and merges the two. Pull is cheap here because you follow only a handful of celebrities, and their latest posts are hot and easy to cache.
steps.idea: Push for the many small authors, pull for the few huge ones, merge at read time.
steps.caption: The feed service merges the cached ID list with fresh celebrity posts.

steps.title: The ranking stage
steps.body: A newest-first list is simple, but most products rank posts by how interesting they are. Scoring every post you could ever see is too slow, so ranking is a second stage. The feed service gathers a few hundred candidates (cached IDs plus celebrity posts). The ranker scores only those, using signals like recency, how often you interact with the author, and how popular the post is. It returns the top 20. Gathering candidates is cheap and wide; ranking is costly and narrow.
steps.idea: Candidate generation is cheap and wide; ranking is expensive and narrow, so keep them separate.
steps.caption: The ranker scores a few hundred candidates and returns the top page.

steps.title: A cache node dies
steps.body: The feed cache is a copy built from other data, not the source of truth, so losing a node loses no posts. For affected users the feed service finds a missing list and rebuilds it by pulling recent posts from the people they follow, then saves the result back in the cache. A rebuild is slow, so it is rate limited and often done lazily, on the user's next visit. It also gives a cheap policy for inactive users: skip pushing to them and rebuild only if they return.
steps.idea: Treat feeds as rebuildable caches: pull is the fallback that makes push safe to lose.
steps.caption: A missing list is rebuilt with a slower pull, then cached again.

steps.title: When to do the work
steps.body: Pull builds feeds when you read: cheap writes, slow reads. Push builds them when someone posts, into a per-user list of IDs in cache: fast reads, but write cost grows with the number of followers. Celebrities break push, so the hybrid pushes for normal accounts and pulls for huge ones. A ranker then scores a few hundred candidates, and the cache can always be rebuilt from the post store.
steps.idea: Move work from the hot read path to the write path, except where the write cost explodes.
steps.caption: Push for most accounts, pull for celebrities, rank a shortlist.

quiz.q: Reads outnumber writes about 10 to 1 and most users follow around 200 accounts. Why is fan-out on write usually preferred for these users?
options: It uses less total storage than pulling
It does the merge work once per post, instead of once per feed load
It guarantees every follower sees the post instantly
It removes the need for a post store
quiz.why: With many more reads than writes, doing the work once at write time (200 small inserts) beats redoing a 200-way merge on each of the 10 reads.

quiz.q: An account with 30 million followers posts. Pure fan-out on write would do what?
options: Make 30 million cache writes for one post, creating a large backlog
Make one write, because the cache is shared
Fail the post until followers come online
Have no effect on other users' posts
quiz.why: Push cost equals follower count, so one post means about 30 million writes, delaying fan-out for everyone queued behind it.

quiz.q: In the hybrid design, how does a user's feed include a celebrity's post?
options: The celebrity's post is pushed to the user's list as usual
The feed service pulls recent celebrity posts at read time and merges them with the cached list
The user's app polls the celebrity's profile directly
Celebrity posts are shown only if the user refreshes twice
quiz.why: Celebrities are skipped during fan-out. At read time the feed service fetches their latest posts and merges them with the pushed list.

quiz.q: Why does the ranker score only a few hundred candidates instead of every post from followed accounts?
options: Ranking models cannot handle more than 300 inputs
The cache can only hold 300 IDs per user
Users never scroll past 300 posts
Scoring is expensive per item, so a cheap first stage narrows the set within the latency budget
quiz.why: Candidate generation is cheap and wide, ranking is costly per post. Limiting the scored set keeps the feed load within its latency budget.

quiz.q: A feed cache node is lost. What is the right recovery approach?
options: Restore from the ranker's output
Declare the affected users' posts lost and notify them
Rebuild each affected list by pulling from the post store, ideally lazily and rate limited
Stop all new posts until the node returns
quiz.why: The cache is derived data. The post store is the source of truth, so lists can be rebuilt by pull, throttled so a rebuild storm does not overload the store.

cheatsheet.def: On each new post, insert its ID into every follower's feed list ahead of time. Fast reads, write cost grows with follower count.
Build the feed at request time by querying and merging the posts of everyone followed. Cheap writes, slow and costly reads.
Accounts with millions of followers make push write millions of entries per post. Handle them with pull instead.
Push for normal accounts, pull for accounts above a follower threshold, merged by the feed service at read time.
Per-user capped list of recent post IDs (not bodies) in memory, about 4 KB for 500 IDs. Derived data that can be rebuilt.
The cheap first stage that gathers a few hundred possible posts before the ranker scores them.
A model scoring candidates on recency, affinity and engagement, returning the top page. Costly per item, so run on a shortlist.
100M posts/day is about 1,160 posts/s; times 200 followers is about 230K cache writes/s. Divide per-day numbers by 86,400.

lab.prompt: Design the news feed for a social app with 100 million daily users. Users follow about 200 accounts on average, a small number of accounts have over 10 million followers, and a feed must load in under 500 ms at p99. Sketch the write path, the read path, and what is stored where.
requirements: Posting returns quickly and does not wait for followers' feeds to update
Feed loads meet a 500 ms p99 target at roughly 12K reads per second average
Accounts with tens of millions of followers must not stall fan-out for everyone else
Feeds can be ranked, not only sorted by time
Losing a feed cache node must not lose any posts
State your assumptions and compute writes per second and cache memory
hints: Convert per day to per second by dividing by about 86,400, then multiply posts per second by average followers.
Store post IDs, not post bodies, in the feed list; keep bodies in the post store and batch the lookup.
Pick a follower threshold for pull accounts, and say what happens to a user who follows both kinds.
Split feed building into candidate generation and ranking so each has its own latency budget.
Ask what to do for inactive users: do you push to them at all?
checklist: Post path: save to post store first, then enqueue fan-out asynchronously
Feed list stored as a capped per-user list of post IDs in cache with a size estimate
Hybrid rule: push for normal accounts, pull and merge for celebrity accounts
Ranking stage scores a few hundred candidates and returns a top page
Recovery plan: rebuild lists from the post store, throttled
Numbers shown: about 1.2K posts/s, about 230K push writes/s, about 400 GB of feed cache
